title: Knee-point finder: quant economics & mini-calculator notes
body:
Context and goal:
This is a working note for a light-weight "knee-point" heuristic and an associated spreadsheet layout that helps engineers pick quantization targets (INT8 / FP8 / 4-bit hybrid) based on three signals: incremental cost savings, measured latency impact, and measured quality (∆EMB / ∆NLG / task-specific metric). The aim is not to replace eval suites but to provide a quick, explainable decision aid for engineers and PMs when balancing unit economics vs SLA risk.

Intended audience:
- ML engineers doing model-onboarding for Redwood Optimize recommendations
- Product PMs and solutions engs who want a quick recommendation for deployment tiers
- SRE/infra to sanity check latency budgets and fallback policies

High level idea (one-liner):
Find where the marginal cost savings per marginal unit of quality degradation crosses an acceptability threshold — that crossing is the "knee". Prefer quantization configurations at or just before that knee unless latency breakeven forces otherwise.

How to use this doc:
1) Run small eval sweep: baseline fp16 (or customer baseline), INT8, FP8, 4-bit (e.g., GPT-like 4-bit quant) across representative prompt set
2) Collect: cost_per_token_estimate, median p95 latency (ms) at target batch size, quality hit (task-specific: accuracy/ROUGE/embedding-cosine drop)
3) Paste numbers into the spreadsheet layout below and inspect knee metric + latency deltas
4) Use the knee-point rule to choose candidate quant profile and then run full eval/QA on a holdout prompt set

Spreadsheet layout (columns to include):
- config_label (string): e.g. baseline-fp16, int8-qdq, fp8-tuned, 4bit-mixed
- model_size (string): e.g. 7B, 13B, 70B
- tokens_per_second_serving (num): observed throughput at production packing/batching
- p95_latency_ms (num): median p95 over short run
- cost_per_1M_tokens_usd (num): unit economics estimate (include infra amortization and SW stack multiplier)
- quality_metric (num): unified quality score (normalized to baseline=100)
- delta_quality_vs_baseline (num): 100 - quality_metric (so higher is worse)
- delta_cost_percent (num): 100 * (baseline_cost - config_cost)/baseline_cost
- marginal_savings_per_quality_drop (num): formula below
- recommended_flag (string): blank / consider / avoid

Key formulas (spreadsheet-friendly text you can paste):
- delta_quality_vs_baseline = baseline_quality - quality_metric
- delta_cost_percent = 100 * (baseline_cost_per_1M_tokens - cost_per_1M_tokens) / baseline_cost_per_1M_tokens
- marginal_savings_per_quality_drop = delta_cost_percent / (delta_quality_vs_baseline + 0.001)
  - interpret: percent cost saved per percent quality lost; high is attractive but watch absolute quality drop

Knee-point algorithm (simple, explainable):
1) Order configs by delta_quality_vs_baseline ascending (best-quality-first)
2) Compute marginal_savings_per_quality_drop for each step compared to previous better-quality config
3) Smooth marginal_savings using a 3-point moving median to avoid noise from microbenching
4) The knee is the last configuration where marginal_savings_per_quality_drop >= threshold_T (heuristic).
   - Suggested default threshold_T = 2.0 (i.e., at least 2% cost saving per 1% quality loss).
   - Lower threshold for high-SLA products (T = 0.5), higher for cost-sensitive (T = 4.0)
5) If a config increases p95_latency_ms by > latency_budget_increase (e.g., +20% relative) mark as avoid even if knee says consider

Why this heuristic?
- It trades off relative (percent) savings against relative quality loss, making it comparable across model sizes and workloads.
- Threshold_T encapsulates product risk tolerance and is easy to explain to PMs.
- Smoothing prevents one-off noisy runs from selecting aggressive configs.

Example tiny dataset (paste into sheet to sanity-check):
Rows: baseline-fp16, int8-default, fp8-tuned, 4bit-mixed
- baseline-fp16: model_size=13B, tokens_per_second=120, p95_latency_ms=150, cost_per_1M_tokens_usd=12.0, quality_metric=100.0
- int8-default: model_size=13B, tokens_per_second=140, p95_latency_ms=155, cost_per_1M_tokens_usd=7.8, quality_metric=98.6
- fp8-tuned: model_size=13B, tokens_per_second=138, p95_latency_ms=152, cost_per_1M_tokens_usd=6.9, quality_metric=98.9
- 4bit-mixed: model_size=13B, tokens_per_second=165, p95_latency_ms=210, cost_per_1M_tokens_usd=3.6, quality_metric=94.0

Compute quick metrics (hand example):
- baseline -> int8: delta_quality = 1.4, delta_cost_percent = 35.0, marginal_savings_per_quality_drop ~ 25.0 -> very attractive, likely before knee
- int8 -> fp8: delta_quality = -0.3 (i.e., fp8 slightly better on this run), delta_cost_percent = 11.5 (fp8 cheaper than int8) -> smoothing needed; interpret as fp8 dominates int8 in both cost and quality here
- fp8 -> 4bit: delta_quality = 4.9, delta_cost_percent = 47.8, marginal_savings_per_quality_drop ~ 9.8 -> big drop in quality for large savings, may be past knee for high-SLA apps

Latency guardrails:
- absolute p95 must be <= product_p95_slo (eg 250 ms). If config violates SLA, mark avoid.
- relative_latency_ratio = p95_config / p95_baseline; if > 1.2, require heavier scrutiny and QA runs

Decision rubric (example):
- recommended_flag = "consider" if config is at or before knee AND relative_latency_ratio <= 1.15 AND delta_quality_vs_baseline <= 3.0
- recommended_flag = "avoid" if delta_quality_vs_baseline > 7.0 OR relative_latency_ratio > 1.3 OR p95_absolute > SLA
- recommended_flag = "experimental" for 4-bit configs that save >40% cost but drop quality 3-7% (run longer eval)

Practical notes and gotchas (from prior sweeps):
- Mixed 4-bit packing can sometimes improve throughput dramatically but increases memory pressure and kernel variance leading to p95 spikes; include repeated short-run p95 samples rather than single-run numbers
- FP8 behavior varies more by model arch and kernel library (AVX vs CUDA kernel maturity) — profile both throughput and numerical stability on critical prompts (dates, numbers, code)
- Embedding metrics need different framing: small cosine drops can be amplified at scale (downstream index quality) so treat embedding quality drop tolerance as lower (threshold 1% instead of 3%)

Operational next steps (todo list):
- [ ] Convert this layout into an actual Google Sheet template (columns + sample formulas) and attach to confluence page OPT-quant-playbook-1432 (owner: Liam)
- [ ] Add an automated microbench harness to produce the tokens_per_second and p95_latency_ms metrics on target infra (owner: Marco)
- [ ] Run 3 pilot sweeps for 7B and 13B models across two customer workload clusters to calibrate threshold_T (owner: Aisha)
- [ ] Draft short README for Solutions Engs describing how to run the fast-sweep and interpret the knee output (owner: Eve)

Open questions for the team (needs discussion in #quantization-discuss):
- Should the knee metric be expressed in absolute $/quality-drop rather than percent? Pros: easier for finance; Cons: less portable across model sizes
- Do we want to incorporate model-variance risk (stddev of quality across prompts) into the knee computation? Tentative: yes, weight configs by 1/(1+stddev)
- For embedding-heavy customers, should we use a separate threshold_T_embed (lower) and an embedding-specific binder sheet?

Quick links (placeholders):
- Confluence playbook: confluence:OPT-quant-playbook-1432
- Existing spreadsheet drafts: google-sheet:1a2b3c-quant-econ-proto (owner: Marco)
- Related PR: github:repo/quant-calcs/pull/58

Notes to self:
- keep the heuristic simple enough for PMs to justify in slides but detailed enough for ML to reproduce
- make sure any recommended_flag includes a short rationale cell in the sheet (1–2 short sentences)

End of notes.
